title: BTFL: A Bayesian-based Test-Time Generalization Method for Internal and External Data Distributions in Federated learning

problem.claim: Online federated learning must handle distribution shifts and evolving test samples while balancing personalization and generalization during testing.

gap.claim: Existing methods primarily focus on training-phase generalization and personalized federated learning struggles with out-of-distribution test samples.

contributions.claim: Introduces Test-time Generalization for Internal and External Distributions in Federated Learning (TGFL), evaluating adaptability under internal and external distributions.
Proposes BTFL, a Bayesian-based test-time generalization method that balances generalization and personalization at the sample level during testing.
Uses a two-head architecture and dual-Bayesian prediction interpolation to combine local and global knowledge using historical test data and current sample characteristics.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report improved performance across various datasets and models with less time cost.
The authors report that source code is publicly available.

narrative_sequence.summary: Federated learning enables collaborative global-model development while maintaining data privacy.
Online deployment encounters distribution shifts, evolving test samples, and a personalization-generalization trade-off, especially for out-of-distribution samples.
The paper defines TGFL to evaluate test-time adaptability across internal and external distributions.
BTFL applies sample-level Bayesian balancing through two heads and dual-Bayesian prediction interpolation.
Experiments are reported to improve performance with lower time cost, and source code is made publicly available.

source_observation.claim: The method separates local and global knowledge and combines them using both historical test data and current sample characteristics.

interpretation.claim: Test-time adaptation may benefit from combining persistent knowledge with sample-specific evidence.

application.claim: For systems facing changing data distributions, consider architectures that preserve distinct general and personalized representations before adaptive fusion.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this design transfers beyond federated learning or which distribution shifts it handles best.

unknowns: Dataset identities, model configurations, baselines, and quantitative results are not specified.
Theoretical guarantee details and the meaning of faster speed are not specified.
The distinction between internal and external distributions is not operationally defined.
